'''Bernard Morris Dwork''' (May 27, 1923 – May 9, 1998) was an American [[mathematician]], known for his application of [[p-adic analysis|''p''-adic analysis]] to [[local zeta function]]s, and in particular for a proof of the first part of the [[Weil conjectures]]: the rationality of the zeta function of a [[algebraic variety|variety]] over a [[finite field]]. The general theme of Dwork's research was ''p''-adic [[cohomology]] and ''p''-adic [[differential equation]]s. He published two papers under the pseudonym Maurizio Boyarsky.

==Career==
Dwork studied electrical engineering at the [[City College of New York]] and [[Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute]].<ref name="princeton-obit">{{cite web |url=https://pr.princeton.edu/pwb/98/0525/0525-2a.html |title=Bernard Dwork Obituary |series= Princeton Weekly Bulletin |date=May 25, 1998 |website=[[Princeton University]] |access-date=October 25, 2023}}</ref> He served in the [[Pacific War|Pacific theater of World War II]].<ref name="princeton-obit"/>

He received his Ph.D. at [[Columbia University]] in 1954 under direction of [[Emil Artin]] (his formal advisor was [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]]); [[Nick Katz]] was one of his students.<ref name=ams /><ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=13357}}.</ref>

He spent 3 years at [[Harvard University]] and 7 years at [[Johns Hopkins University]] before joining [[Princeton University]] as a faculty member in 1964.<ref name="princeton-obit"/> He became Eugene Higgins Professor of Mathematics in 1978 and became emeritus in 1993.<ref name="princeton-obit"/> He was named a Professore di Chiara Fama by the Italian government and held a special chair at the [[University of Padua]] from 1992 onwards.<ref name="princeton-obit"/>

==Awards and honors==
For his proof of the first part of the Weil conjectures, Dwork received (together with [[Kenkichi Iwasawa]]) the [[Cole Prize]] in 1962.<ref name=ams>[https://www.ams.org/notices/199903/mem-dwork.pdf Memorial article] – by [[Nick Katz]] and [[John Tate (mathematician)|John Tate]].</ref> He received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] in  [[List of Guggenheim Fellowships awarded in 1964|1964]].<ref name=ams />

==Personal life==
Dwork was married to Shirley Dwork and is the father of computer scientist [[Cynthia Dwork]], historian [[Deborah Dwork]], and Andrew Dwork.<ref name="princeton-obit"/>
